text: Real-time assessment of hybridization between wolves and dogs: combining noninvasive samples with ancestry informative markers

Wolves and dogs provide a paradigmatic example of the ecological and conservation implications of hybridization events between wild and domesticated forms. However, our understanding of such implications has been traditionally hampered by both high genetic similarity and the difficulties in obtaining tissue samples (TS), which limit our ability to assess ongoing hybridization events. To assess the occurrence and extension of hybridization in a pack of wolf-dog hybrids in northwestern Iberia, we compared the power of 52 nuclear markers implemented on TS with a subset of 13 ancestry informative markers (AIMs) typed in noninvasive samples (NIS). We demonstrate that the 13 AIMs are as accurate as the 52 markers that were chosen without regard to the power to differentiate between wolves and dogs, also having the advantage of being rapidly screened on NIS. The efficiency of AIMs significantly outperformed ten random sets of similar size and an additional commercial set of 18 markers. Bayesian clustering analysis implemented on AIMs and NIS identified nine hybrids, two wolves and two dogs. Four hybrids were unambiguously assigned to F1xWolf backcrosses. Our approach (AIMs + NIS) overcomes previous difficulties related to sample availability and informative power of markers, allowing a quick identification of wolf-dog hybrids in the first phases of hybridization episodes. This provides managers with a reliable tool to evaluate hybridization and estimate the success of their actions. This approach may be easily adapted for other pairs of wild/domesticated species, thus improving our understanding of the introgression of domestication genes into natural populations.

Hybridization is increasingly recognized as a powerful evolutionary force promoting speciation (Soltis & Soltis 2009), shaping adaptation through introgressive hybridization (Kays et al. 2010) or yielding evolutionary novelties (Godinho et al. 2008). However, hybridization can also pose a risk to species, particularly non-natural hybridization (Rhymer & Simberloff 1996;Allendorf et al. 2001), turning this process into the focus of attention within conservation and management disciplines and leading to an intense and controversial debate in recent times (e.g. Wolf et al. 2001;Haig et al. 2004;Fitzpatrick et al. 2010;Stronen & Paquet 2013).
Climate change (Garroway et al. 2010), species translocation, introduction or invasion (Kidd et al. 2009), and habitat transformation (Mullen et al. 2012) or human pressure (Rutledge et al. 2012) are increasing the chances for hybridization and genetic introgression between closely related species, including between wild and domestic forms (Randi 2008). The latter is considered a very worrying type of hybridization for wild species due to the consequences of intensive artificial selection in domestic stocks to conform to human interests and is expected to increase the probability for accumulation of deleterious alleles, as well as to disrupt co-adapted gene complexes or local adaptations in wild populations (Allendorf et al. 2001;Randi 2008).
A classic example of the conservation implications of this process is the hybridization between wolves (Canis lupus) and its domestic form, the dog (Canis l. familiaris).
In particular, the idea that the spread of domestication genes into wolf populations could disrupt local adaptation or increase genetic homogenization through introgressive hybridization soon became a major conservation issue for this charismatic species (Vil a & Wayne 1999;Boitani 2000) and is today the focus of research and conservation interest, especially in Europe (Randi 2011). Several cases of hybridization with dogs have been reported throughout the entire range of the species (Randi 2011), but to date, results appear to suggest that its frequency in the wild is low and few instances of significant introgression of dog genes into wolf populations were described (Randi & Lucchini 2002;Vil a et al. 2003;Verardi et al. 2006;Godinho et al. 2011;Hindrikson et al. 2012; but see Anderson et al. 2009).
However, the extremely high genetic similarity between wolves and dogs (Wayne & vonHoldt 2012) makes the detection of hybrids a difficult task, which is exacerbated by the fact that wolf-dog hybrids can exhibit typical dog or wolf phenotypes. This problem could be partially solved using biparental molecular markers, but their effectiveness appears to be strongly dependent on both the number (see V€ ah€ a & Primmer 2006) and availability of accurate allelic and genotypic frequencies in reference populations (e.g. 'pure' wolves and dogs), a crucial issue when applying Bayesian clustering to detect hybridization (Anderson & Thompson 2002;Falush et al. 2003).
A major conservation concern is the low chance of detecting hybridization events, which, to date, have been essentially anecdotal reports (e.g. casual observations, roadkills, poaching or hunting of suspected individuals). For a correct assessment of these cases, obtaining tissue samples (TS) from the animals is usually needed (but see Bohling & Waits 2011;and Caniglia et al. 2013). Consequently, because obtaining TS from wolves is often difficult, our ability to assess the occurrence of wolf-dog hybridizations in real time and its extension at a population level is still very limited. This is unfortunate because repercussions on our understanding of the ecological, evolutionary and conservation implications of this process are substantial. For example, from a management point of view, the invasive nature and difficulty of collecting TS from a representative number of individuals limit our ability to evaluate the occurrence and extent of hybridization in real time, which can lead to significant delays in management efforts to mitigate their potential effects. In this respect, ecologists must provide managers with reliable, quick and efficient tools to evaluate the occurrence of hybridization and its importance at a population level.
The alternative to address this task is the use of noninvasive samples (NIS). Although the use of NIS has grown extraordinarily in recent years (Long et al. 2008), their application to detect hybridization is still rare (Bohling & Waits 2011;Rutledge et al. 2012;Caniglia et al. 2013), and the optimization of results for detecting wolfdog hybrids is far from achieved. Here, we test the utility of NIS to assist conservation practitioners in the management of wolf-dog hybridization. To do so, we use already available NIS and TS samples from a canid pack composed of wolves and hybrids in northwestern Iberia. Our main objectives are to evaluate the utility of NIS (i) for a quick detection of hybridization at both individual and population levels and (ii) to estimate the genetic composition of individuals and identify their respective hybrid classes. To do this, we compare the power of a set of 52 nuclear markers, including those described in Godinho et al. (2011) for TS, with a second one of 13 markers we selected for NIS. Our panel of 13 markers is based on their ancestry informative power, and offers a fast and inexpensive solution to study ongoing hybridization events.

We used as case study a canid pack located in the Sierra del Barbanza (42°42 0 N-8°56 0 W), a mountainous area (ca. 416 km 2 ; 0-600 m.a.s.l) in northwestern Iberia (Galicia; Fig. 1b,c), where wolves have been present at least during the last four decades in a human-dominated landscape (Llaneza et al. 2012a), feeding mainly on livestock, particularly cattle and horses (Guiti an et al. 1979;L opez-Bao et al. 2013). In this area, feral dogs are thought to be numerous although no population estimates exist. In 2011, field observations (A. Perez, personal communication) and a subsequent study funded by the Regional Government of Galicia showed the pack included both wolves and wolf-dog hybrids (Godinho et al. 2012;Fig. 1a). As a consequence, in the same year, based on general management recommendations of wolf-dog hybridization events (Boitani 2000), stakeholders decided for the removal of putative hybrids from the field (two in July and two in September 2011, a male and a female each time; Godinho et al. 2012).
Between August and September 2011, we collected 38 wolf-like scats along existing paths, forest trails and firebreaks, where the probability of territorial marks detection is maximized (Llaneza et al. 2014). Samples were collected during four different surveys (at least 1 week interval between surveys, 2 days per survey) corresponding to a total sampled distance of about 35 km per sampling (ca. 105 km in total). All scats compatible with wolf-like canids were collected, which increased the chance of collecting scats from red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) and dogs. Both TS from the four putative hybrids and NIS were stored at room temperature in sterile tubes containing approximately four parts of 96% ethanol.

DNA from TS was extracted using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA) according to manufacturer's instructions. The same extraction procedure was used for reference samples (242 wolves and 237 dogs). Reference wolves were obtained from dead animals (mainly roadkills and legal hunting) collected between 1996 and 2012 and were selected to allow a maximum of two wolves per pack/generation across the Iberian range (Fig. 1b). All wolf samples carried an Iberian mtDNA haplotype (Vil a et al. 1999;Godinho et al. 2011) and were classified according to the Euclidean distance to Barbanza in three groups: <10 km (n = 17), 10-50 km (n = 19) and >50 km (n = 206). Reference dogs were comprised of stray dogs (n = 45) and a random selection of samples including (i) six Iberian herding breeds (Serra da Estrela, n = 28; Castro Laboreiro, n = 24; Cão de Gado Transmontano, n = 22; Rafeiro do Alentejo, n = 25; Fila de São Miguel, n = 15; Serra de Aires, n = 13), (ii) three hound breeds (Portuguese Water Dog, n = 8; Podengo Português, n = 25; Perdigueiro Português, n = 26) and (iii) German Shepherd (n = 6). Reference dogs carried dog mtDNA haplotypes (Vil a et al. 1999;Godinho et al. 2011).
DNA was extracted from faecal samples following Frantz et al. (2003) protocol after applying the GuSCN⁄silica method (Boom et al. 1990). Subsequently, PCR inhibitors were removed from samples using the Microcon â YM-30 centrifugal Filter System (Millipore, Billerica, MA). All pre-PCR procedures were carried out in a dedicated laboratory used only for the manipulation of lowquality DNA under sterile conditions and positive air pressure. Negative controls were included throughout the entire process to test for DNA contamination. The quality of noninvasive DNA was assessed based on the amplification of one high-copy DNA target (420 bp of the mtDNA HVI region; Vil a et al. 1999) and four amplification replicates of three low-copy DNA targets (microsatellites). Samples exhibiting dog or Iberian wolf mitochondrial haplotypes (n = 25) and successful amplification of the four markers were analysed further.

Individual multilocus genotypes were determined for TS using a set of 52 nuclear loci selected across the genome without regard to the degree to which they differentiate wolves and dogs, and for NIS using a subset of 13 ancestry informative markers (AIMs) of the initial 52 loci. The 13 markers were specifically selected based on (i) the magnitude of F ST values between wolf and dog for 11 markers and (ii) the probability of identity (PID) for two additional loci to ensure unequivocal individual identification.
Fourty-two of the 52 loci matched to the panel screened by Godinho et al. (2011), and the same methodology was applied. The remaining 10 loci include eight microsatellites, one single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in intron 2 of solute carrier family 24 member 5 gene (SLC24A5) and a 5 bp deletion at intron 3 of the KIT ligand gene (KITLG) (see Appendix S1 for a complete description of new markers and primers). Additionally, scats were screened for a molecular sexing test following Seddon (2005).
For each TS, 50 microsatellites were amplified in five multiplex reactions, while for NIS, 11 microsatellites and the 5 bp deletion of KITLG were amplified in two multiplex reactions (see Appendix S2 for markers description, multiplex sets and PCR conditions). Each locus was amplified and genotyped four different times for each scat sample to minimize errors. Amplifications were performed using the QIAGEN Multiplex PCR Kit (except for Finnzymes Canine Genotypes Panel 1.1) following the manufacturer's instructions and using a 10 ll final volume and negative controls to monitor possible contaminants. Fluorescent labelling of PCR fragments was accomplished following Blacket et al. (2002). PCR products were separated by size on an ABI3130xl DNA analyzer. Alleles were determined using GENEMAPPER 4.1 (Applied Biosystems) and checked manually by two observers. For scat samples, the consensus genotypes over the four replicas were determined following three rules: (i) heterozygous genotypes were accepted if the same genotype was observed in two independent PCRs; (ii) homozygous genotypes were accepted if the genotype was observed in three independent PCRs; and (iii) samples that failed to amplify at four or more loci were removed from further analysis.
Successful amplifications for the SLC24A5 and mtDNA fragments were sequenced in both directions following the BigDye chemistry (Applied Biosystems), and sequencing products were separated in the same DNA analyzer. Sequences were aligned and compared in the software SEQSCAPE 2.0 (Applied Biosystems), and any discrepancies re-assessed. Data were deposited in Gen-Bank (see Data Accessibility for Accession numbers).

Data sets with 52 and 13 markers were analysed in parallel for all procedures in order to evaluate the power of the subset selected for NIS. Genetic diversity was evaluated for wolves and dogs (Barbanza individuals were excluded) based on allele frequencies and observed (Ho) and expected (He) heterozygosities for each locus at each population using ARLEQUIN 3.5.1.2 (Excoffier et al. 2005).
The same software was used to test for deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and significance of association between genotypes at pairs of loci in each population (LD). The level of statistical significance was adjusted using strict Bonferroni corrections (Rice 1989). Allelic richness (AR) and private allelic richness (PrAR) per population were estimated using the rarefaction algorithm implemented in ADZE 1.0 (Szpiech et al. 2008) after standardizing to the smallest sample size (N = 224).
ARLEQUIN was also used to estimate genetic differentiation between wolves and dogs through a hierarchical analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA) using h analogues of Wright's F-statistics. Significance of genetic differentiation was tested by random permutations, under the null hypothesis that all individuals belong to a single population.
Multiple identical genotypes from NIS were identified and excluded from analysis as they are likely from the same individual. The mean allelic dropout and false allele amplification values across loci for the 13-loci data set were evaluated using GIMLET (Vali ere 2002). Individual genotypes of 242 reference wolves and 237 reference dogs were analysed using the Bayesian clustering procedure implemented in STRUCTURE 2.3.3 (Falush et al. 2003) assuming two populations (K = 2) and including a set of previously validated wolf and dog samples (Godinho et al. 2011). The STRUCTURE analysis was performed independently 20 times for 10 6 permutations after a burn-in period of 10 5 permutations using the admixture model with correlated allele frequencies among populations and no priors for individual identification (POPFLAG=0). The average membership proportion (Qi) for wolf and dog reference samples and the individual membership proportions (q i ) to the inferred clusters and their 90% probability intervals (CI) were assessed in each run of STRUCTURE. The same analysis was repeated including Barbanza individuals, but this time considering each parental class as a separate entity (POPFLAG=1) and turning on the option PFROMPOPFLAGONLY to update allele frequencies throughout the run using only reference individuals, causing the qi estimate for each unknown individual dependent only on the reference set and not on other unknown individuals in the sample (Pritchard et al. 2010).
The power of admixture analyses to distinguish parental from hybrid classes and to establish the range of expected q-values for admixed generations was assessed for both the 52 loci and the 13 AIMs by simulating both parental and hybrid genotypes in HYBRIDLAB v.1.0 (Nielsen et al. 2006; named STRUCTURE-training by Latch et al. (2011). Genotypes of 100 wolves and 100 dogs with q-values greater than 0.98 (training data set) were used to generate 1000 of each parental genotypes.
The results were then used to simulate 1000 of each F 1 and first and second backcross genotypes to both wolves and dogs. Simulated genotypes were then submitted to admixture analyses with STRUCTURE using the same model and settings described above (10 5 burn-in, 10 6 iterations, admixture model, correlated allele frequencies, POPFLAG=0). In addition, we compared the results obtained for our set of AIMs with 10 subsets of 13 randomly selected markers from the initial set of 52 to test its performance. We also carried out a comparison with the set of 18 microsatellites available as a single multiplex on the Finnzymes commercial kit. These subsets were checked for genetic diversity, probability of identity (PID), probability of identity between siblings (PIDsibs; using GIMLET) and differentiation between 1000 simulated wolves and 1000 simulated dogs. All subsets were also run on STRUCTURE (10 5 burnin, 10 6 iterations, admixture model, correlated allele frequencies, POPFLAG=0) for estimation of the average population assignment (Qi), range of individual assignments (qi range) and 90% probability intervals (CI) for both wolves and dogs. As an indicator of effectiveness, we also calculated the proportion of wolves with qi wolf below 0.95 and the proportion of dogs with qi Dog below 0.90. Statistical differences between the Qi Wolf obtained using the selected AIMs and each of the Qi Wolf generated by each randomly selected subset of 13 markers, as well as the Finnzymes set, were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests. We further tested for differences in the proportion of wolves with qi < 0.95 between the selected AIMs and the 11 subsets of markers using a two-samples proportion test.
A detailed analysis of hybrid ancestry was conducted using NEWHYBRIDS 1.1 (Anderson & Thompson 2002). The posterior probability of assignment (qi) to seven genotype frequency classes (wolf, dog, F 1 , and first and second-generation backcrosses to wolves and dogs) was estimated for each Barbanza individual using prior population information for reference samples. Settings used were 10 6 MCMC permutations following 10 5 burn-in steps, no information for allele frequencies and Jeffreystype priors for both mixing proportions and allele frequencies.
To evaluate the proportion of individuals studied at Barbanza, we also estimated the number of individuals in the area using the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) implemented in the 'capwire' R package (Pennell et al. 2013). This is a capture-recapture method that accounts for the fact that individuals can be 'captured' more than once per sampling session using NIS. We used the equal capture model (ECM) and performed a parametric bootstrap (1000 bootstraps) to estimate 95% CI for the MLE.

Individual identification at the Barbanza pack using NIS MtDNA sequences were obtained from 35 wolf-like scats (92.1%), from which 25 (71.4%) were assigned to the Iberian wolf haplotype W7 (Vali ere et al. 2003), four to the dog (11.4%) and six to the red fox (17.2%). Individual identifications of scat samples resulted in 62.1% success, representing 18 of the 29 wolf or dog mtDNA identifications. Mean values of allelic dropout and false alleles amplification across loci (12.3% and 1.0%, respectively) and across samples (13.0% and 0.8%) were under the average expected values for noninvasive genetic studies (Broquet et al. 2007).
Overall, between July and September 2011, we identified 13 individuals, 10 of them using NIS (individual TS4 was identified using both methods; Table 2). We could determine the sex in eight NIS, identifying in total (including TS) eight females and four males (Table 2). The MLE-estimated census size in Barbanza area was 14 (95% bootstrap CI: 11-20 individuals; dogs were excluded from the analysis), suggesting that we sampled a significant fraction of the estimated population (80%).

section: comparing diversity and differentiation for 52 and 13 loci
text:
The comparison between 52-and 13-loci data sets for genetic diversity of Iberian wolves and dogs showed contrasting results. The 52-loci data set showed higher genetic diversity for all measured statistics, for both wolves and dogs, including mean number of alleles per locus, allelic richness and expected heterozygosity (Table 1). Nonetheless, values achieved with 13 loci for the private allelic richness were very similar, for both wolves and dogs, conforming the expectations of retaining loci that maximize differentiation (Table 1). Regardless of the data set, Iberian wolves exhibited lower genetic diversity values for all parameters when compared to dogs (see Appendix S3 for individual diversity and differentiation measures for the 13 AIMs). When analysing wolves and dogs separately, we did not observe any significant LD pairwise combinations (significance probability level P < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for 132 comparisons) or deviations from Hardy-Weinberg expectations (P < 0.01) for any loci. This observation likely results from the selection of wolf reference samples avoiding familiar relationships, and the same applies to both stray and purebred dogs.
Population pairwise F ST-52 (0.193) and F ST-13 (0.341) over loci revealed a highly significant genetic differentiation between wolves and dogs (P < 0.0001; Table 1) for both data sets. Nonetheless, the larger F ST value exhibited by the selected 13 loci shows a greater effectiveness to differentiate the two gene pools. Our AMOVA results also showed that a high proportion of genetic diversity was explained by variation between populations in both data sets (19.90% for 52 loci, 35.86% for 13 loci).

Bayesian clustering analyses performed with reference samples showed concordant results for both 52 and 13 sets of loci and a similar power to sharply differentiate wolves from dogs (Table 2; Figs 2 and3). The average proportion of membership to the wolf cluster was similar for both data sets (Qi 52 = 0.998 and Qi 13 = 0.997; Table 2), with qi-values ranging between 0.977 < qi 52 < 1.000 and 0.965 < qi 13 < 0.998. Only three and six out of 242 reference wolves presented the minimum value of the 90% CI below 0.90 for 52-and 13-loci data sets, respectively (minimum CI 52 = 0.879 and minimum CI 13 = 0.818). Notably, the 37 wolves collected <50 km to Barbanza evidenced qi > 0.98 and narrow CIs, reflecting a nonadmixed genetic background for the wolf population in the area. All reference dogs were probabilistically assigned to the dog cluster with very similar performance in both data sets, showing an average proportion of membership of Qi 52 = 0.997 and Qi 13 = 0.993, but larger CI for 13 loci (CI = 0.669-1.000) than for 52 loci (CI = 0.864-1.000; Table 2 and Fig. 2).
The effectiveness of the 13-loci data set was further evaluated using 1000 simulated genotypes from each parental and hybrid class. This STRUCTURE-training procedure revealed average assignments to the correct parental class of qi wolf = 0.967 (minimum qi wolf = 0.910) and qi dog = 0.945 (minimum qi dog = 0.809). Furthermore, only 5% among the 1000 simulated wolf genotypes exhibited a qi wolf < 0.95, while 10% of dog simulated genotypes presented qi dog < 0.90. These Bayesian clustering results obtained with the use of selected AIMs on simulated genotypes of parental classes allowed two different threshold values to be defined for wolves and dogs, respectively, 0.90 and 0.80. Average qi of simulated F 1 genotypes was 0.495 (highest qi F1 = 0.757), and the average qi BxWolf and qi BxDog to their respective clusters was 0.740 and 0.749. For second-generation backcrosses, our battery of loci revealed an average of qi Bx2Wolf and qi Bx2Dog of 0.854 and 0.860, respectively. Based on  defined thresholds, these results suggest that our set of 13 AIMs detect 100% of F 1 individuals, and 96.3% and 66.4% of first-generation backcross individuals to wolf and dog, respectively. For the second-generation backcrosses, the power achieved by this set of loci was 68.2% and 22.8%, respectively, to wolf and dog.

Based on 0.90 and 0.80 thresholds for wolf and dog assignments, respectively, as established using simulated individuals, the clustering assignment of the 13 wolf-like Barbanza individuals clearly showed our data set contained two wolves (qi NIS3 = 0.998 and qi NIS7 = 0.984) and two dogs (qi NIS4 = 0.943 and qi NIS9 = 0.981). The remaining individuals exhibited varying assignments to the wolf cluster equal or below 0.90 (0.905 < qi < 0.670) and wide CI (Table 2). The two wolves and the nine wolf-like individuals exhibited a wolf mitochondrial haplotype, while the two dogs presented dog mtDNA haplotypes. The four analysed TS showed very similar results on clustering analysis with either 52 or 13 loci, although the use of a reduced number of loci slightly shifts the qi-values towards hybridization (Table 2). Analysis of recent ancestry using NEWHYBRIDS for the 13-loci data set confirmed the assignment to parental classes of the two wolves and two dogs previously identified by clustering analysis and further identified one other individual with a high posterior probability of being a wolf (NIS1 = 95.3%; Table 3). Four individuals had a high probability assignment (>80%) of being firstgeneration backcrosses to wolf, while the remaining four were assigned ambiguously to both parental and hybrid classes (Table 3). However, while the use of both sets of nuclear markers showed high agreement at population level, there were slight disagreements at individual level: the four individuals genotyped using TS were undoubtedly identified as second-generation backcrosses to wolf using the 52 loci, while the analysis with the smaller data set assigned two individuals to first-generation backcross to wolf, and the other two were not assigned to any particular hybrid class.

Worldwide, millions of free-ranging dogs coexist with a few tens of thousands of wolves. Consequently, despite biological constraints, there are many opportunities for wolves and dogs hybridize, and cumulative data suggest Fig. 4 Relationship between F ST values and the proportion of wolves with individual assignment (qi) <0.95 (circles) for the selected set of 13 AIMs, the whole set of 52 markers, a commercial panel of 18 markers (Finnzymes) and 10 randomly selected subsets of 13 markers. For each set of markers, proportions were calculated based on 1000 simulated wolves and dogs, respectively. For each set of markers, the observed range in the qi-values is also shown (grey bars).

Ancestry was calculated in NEWHYBRIDS using seven genotype classes [wolf, dog, F 1 , BxWolf (backcross to wolf), BxDog (backcross to dog), Bx2Wolf (second-generation backcross to wolf) and Bx2Dog (second-generation backcross to dog)]. Values in bold indicate probabilities higher than 10% of belonging to a hybrid class 52-loci 13-loci that hybridization may be more frequent than previously suspected (Godinho et al. 2011). Traditionally, hybridization studies have required the slow and generally expensive use of TS collected from dead or trapped animals, thus limiting population-level assessments. Furthermore, difficulties have been reported in correctly identifying wolf-dog backcrosses using simulated individuals and sets of 16-18 microsatellites (Randi 2008), typically resulting in a large threshold implemented in clustering analyses. In contrast, our method avoids these difficulties and is both innovative and easily applicable for hybridization studies. This is because we actively searched for the most informative markers among a previously wellknown extensive set and demonstrate that a small subset of carefully selected 13 AIMs is as accurate as an extensive set of 52 markers, additionally showing a major advantage of being rapidly screened on NIS.
Current studies on wolf-dog hybridization typically consider a set of 11-18 markers (Randi & Lucchini 2002;Vil a et al. 2003;Hindrikson et al. 2012; but see Verardi et al. 2006 for a set of 16 markers arranged in four different linkage groups) to achieve high differentiation values between wolves and dogs (average F ST = 0.28 using Randi &Lucchini 2002 andVerardi et al. 2006). Nonetheless, these studies fail to achieve reliable assignments to recent hybrid classes further than F 1 s using threshold values of 0.80 (but see Caniglia et al. 2013 for a threshold of 0.95 although no available data for the reliability of hybrid classes). In a recent study, Godinho et al. (2011) combined the use of a much larger panel of microsatellites with an assignment study of simulated individuals to reduce the uncertainty on probability intervals, increasing the threshold value to 0.85 and achieving, for the first time, high confidence on identifying first-generation backcross individuals (84% of successful identification). In a similar approach with a panel of 100 unlinked SNP markers, vonHoldt et al. (2013) could detect mixed ancestry within up to four generations of wolf-dog hybridization, although using a threshold of 0.80 and having only 72% of correct identifications of first-generation backcrosses to wolf. Nevertheless, approaches like those, using large numbers of markers, are not currently feasible for low-quality DNA samples, which are often the only ones available for rapid evaluation of a local hybridization event.
Our methods of using 13 nuclear markers specifically selected to have a high differentiation power between Iberian wolves and dogs (F ST of 0.341 for the empirical data and 0.408 for the simulated data) allowed not only a great accuracy in assigning individuals to parental classes (Qi wolf = 0.997) with a threshold that could be safely brought to 90% for assignments to the wolf cluster, but also a high probability of detecting hybrids in empirical cases, including first-generation backcrosses to the wild population. The establishment of a sharp threshold of 90% for this data set, assuming that values below that threshold indicate admixture to the wild population, includes all qi-values for the 242 wolf reference samples and all 1000 simulated wolves, fully supporting our approach. The larger threshold established for assignment to the dog cluster has no consequences on detecting continuous hybridization to wolf and is not a managing concern.
The efficiency of our methodology using 13 AIMs significantly outperformed the ten random sets established for the same number of markers, as well as the set of 18 markers included in the commercial kit, both when using traditional differentiation measures (F ST ) and for Bayesian assignment analysis. However, our AIMs were not more efficient than the whole set of 52 markers for Bayesian assignment analysis (although being more efficient to differentiate populations based on F ST ), confirming expectations that a high number of markers is preferable to a small selected panel. In any case, these results clearly show that selecting informative markers is important when two biological entities involved in hybridization events are very closely related helping on the dilemma of accomplishing this kind of projects with noninvasive samples.
One drawback of our approach is that the use of a small panel of AIMs leads to lower estimates of genetic diversity and, therefore, may not be suitable for some population genetic analyses. On the other hand, allele frequencies may change over time, especially in small populations (e.g. stochastic events, genetic drift, Allee effects, nonrandom mating or selection), which could affect assignment accuracy when studying hybridization. In such cases, selection of molecular markers should be revised over time. Furthermore, the method we propose requires that an extensive list of markers be available for which differences in allele frequencies among the populations under investigation have been estimated. This applies to any species in which our approach would be used and constitutes an additional cost that should be considered before starting a study of hybridization with noninvasive samples.

The Bayesian clustering analysis based on the 13-loci data set identified nine hybrids at Barbanza, together with two wolves and two dogs. Hybrids were assigned to first backcrosses to wolf or were ambiguously assigned to different hybrid classes (Table 3). While the discrepancies on recent ancestry analysis for the Barbanza TS using 13 or 52 loci should be further investigated using simulations, it remains clear that our methods can correctly identify hybrids, which is essential for the effective management of suspicious cases of hybridization. The hybridization event at Barbanza started with a cross between a female wolf and a male dog, as inferred by the presence of an Iberian wolf mtDNA haplotype in all hybrids, corresponding to the typical direction of wolf-dog hybridization (but see Hindrikson et al. 2012). Despite the uncertainty of the impact of these crosses in the genetic composition of wolf populations (for example, due to difficulties of hybrid integration in packs), our results do suggest that the Barbanza pack has quickly evolved towards a hybrid swarm, with a minimum of two generations of backcrossing to wolves. These findings are alarming because wolf packs in nonexpanding populations generally consist of related individuals (Lehman et al. 1992), and thus, other unobserved individuals in the area may also exhibit admixed ancestries.

Efficient identification of wolf-dog hybrids is crucial for the implementation of conservation and management strategies, particularly in the first phases of an episode of hybridization, as well as to evaluate the success of the strategies that have been implemented. Despite the recent increase in the number of studies focusing on this topic, no efficient and effective method for assessing real-time grey wolf-dog hybridization events at the population level has been proposed (although methods have been suggested for other systems like the red wolfcoyote; Bohling et al. 2013). In this regard, our approach of using a small set of AIMs provides managers with a reliable, quick and efficient tool for an intensive and extensive evaluation of hybridization at both individual and population levels. For example, assuming a minimum territory size of 100 km 2 centred in the rendezvous site of the Barbanza pack, the area sampled here covered a substantial portion of that territory (40%; Fig. 1c). Moreover, we identified 11 wolf-like canids (80% of the estimated population), which is fully compatible with the values reported in Iberia for pack size after reproduction (7-9 individuals; Llaneza et al. 2012b) plus some floater animals, suggesting that our method allows a comprehensive evaluation of hybridization in a given area. Our goal to obtain a quick method to identify hybridization events was achieved. Once there is the suspicion of a hybridization event, we estimate that a maximum of 2 months would be required to know the extent of the problem in an area equivalent to a pack territory. Finally, we note that the logistic and economic investment to evaluate hybridization in this area was feasible (ca. 1500€ for the fieldworkone person working 8 daysplus ca. 5000€ for laboratory workone person working 3 weeks).
Current management guidelines state that every practical measure should be implemented to remove obvious hybrids from the wild once an event of hybridization has been detected (Boitani 2000). This implies mainly lethal control, although keeping hybrids in captivity and sterilization have also been suggested (Ciucci 2012). Nevertheless, the efficiency of removing hybrids from the wild remains very uncertain. Therefore, the methods shown here constitute a step forward towards the effective management of wolf-dog hybridization. In our case study, due to the use of NIS coupled with a panel of AIMs, we now know that implemented management actions removed only 44% (four of nine identified hybrids) of wolf-dog hybrids in the region of Barbanza. Thus, we suggest that the combination of NIS and AIMs may offer a great opportunity to better understand the extension and persistence of hybridization between wolves and dogs at a global scale and its ecological, evolutionary and conservation consequences. This approach also brings up the opportunity to evaluate and improve the few existing management guidelines about wolf-dog hybridization.
Finally, our methods may be easily adapted for other pairs of wild/domesticated species, eventually making this an important tool to evaluate the impact of the introgression of domestication genes into natural populations. We believe this is both relevant and timely to examine many situations that have been documented in nature for a variety of species, especially because we now have the genomic and computational tools available which may facilitate this task. For example, the rock pigeon genome has very recently been made available, but the occurrence of true natural populations is questionable (Shapiro et al. 2013), eventually making this the first species to become extinct in the wild through introgressive hybridization with domestic/feral populations (Rhymer & Simberloff 1996). Another remarkable and intriguing example has been described for the wildcat (Felis silvestris) in both Scotland and Hungary, where the extent of introgressive hybridization from domestic breeds may preclude their recovery (Randi 2008). In summary, we suggest that the development and generalized application of the approach described here for the management of wolf-dog hybridization events may offer a very useful tool for conservation biologists in general.
